Division: a US state with a March 2025 facilities statute covering bathrooms, locker rooms, DV shelters, rape crisis centers, dormitories, prisons. Universal exposure — tier 1 state-imposed facility restriction by birth sex. No documented arrest under this statute (unlike the neighboring one with trespass arrest... actually the arrest in parent framework was a different state). Religious refusal statute allows service denial with qualified immunity. No statewide discrimination protection. Risk assessment places it in "Worst" group, second-highest of five, below "Do Not Travel."

Parent framework: passport marker restrictions (X eliminated, M/F per assigned sex), visa adjudication scrutiny, entry screening exposure — but this is a visitor using their own passport from another country... Actually the parent framework here is the country the state belongs to; the visitor enters the country. The parent framework includes document regime affecting travelers: passports blocked/confiscated, visa refusal for document discrepancy, trans travelers stranded abroad. That's a real traveler-facing exposure at border. Also facility bans across states, custody conversion therapy policies in federal prisons, immigration custody abuse.

Wait — but the visitor is entering this country. The parent's border regime applies: trans/nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked at processing; visa officers instructed to refuse where discrepancy in documents casts doubt on sex. That's a significant border exposure. Though that primarily affects... foreign trans travelers whose passports show X marker or mismatched markers. Given the parent's framework: X-marker passports no longer processed; existing X passports valid until expiration. So a visitor with an X passport may face issues? "Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration" — that's for their own nationals. Foreign visitors presenting X markers: Feb 2025 cable instructs refusal where discrepancy casting reasonable doubt on sex. That's a real risk of visa denial/entry refusal for trans travelers. Severity: denial of entry/stranding = level 3.

Facilities: state statute covers bathrooms, locker rooms, shelters, dorms, prisons — universal exposure for the traveler. No documented arrest under it here, but the parent shows an arrest in another state. Rule 15: rate the possibility everyone carries. That's tier 1 exposure without a working remedy (state has no discrimination protection, religious-refusal statute protects denials). Score: similar to 0.35 or 0.45 anchors. Anchors at 0.45: birth-sex bathroom rule in publicly funded buildings, upheld by courts, complaints can't secure access — that's very close to this. Here also shelters, dorms, prisons, plus religious-refusal statute permitting service denial, plus no statewide discrimination protection, plus "Worst" tier rating, plus narrow document route (resident-facing though), plus pending bills.

Also national custody: conversion therapy for trans inmates, immigration custody abuse — a visitor could end up in custody (arrest). Parent's corrections bureau conversion therapy applies federally; state prisons listed in statute scope. Detention placement by sex — state statute includes prisons. That's tier 1 custody placement by birth sex. Combined with parent's federal conversion-therapy-like policy for trans inmates (hair cut, hormones removed). For a visitor arrested, that's severe (level 4).

Hmm — but does the visitor plausibly face custody? Bathrooms arrest possible but not documented under this statute. Still, universal exposure.

Also social climate: religious-refusal statute, senate vote to nullify local ordinances, conservative. Public opinion national: 66% support sex-at-birth documents. Social hostility exists but the record doesn't document violence against trans visitors; hate crime law exists nationally; rule of law functions (courts blocking some measures).

Weighing: tier 1 universal facility exclusion by birth sex across rest stops, shelters, dorms, plus custody placement by birth sex with documented federal hostile custody policy, plus religious-refusal service denial with immunity, plus visa/document border friction for trans visitors, no statewide protections, "Worst" tier. But no criminalisation of trans identity, functioning courts, marriage recognition, employment protection nationally, no documented violence pattern.

Compare 0.35 anchors: e.g., 0.35-A (bathrooms by birth sex in public buildings, complaints rejected, no offence of being trans, polite shops) — this case has facilities bans PLUS custody/shelter/dorm reach PLUS religious refusal immunity PLUS border document exposure PLUS federal custody conversion therapy. That's worse than 0.35-A. 0.25 anchors: e.g., 0.25-D (compulsory birth-sex rule for all public facilities, hospitals wards by sex, visitor complaints rejected, recurrent police stops/extortion). Hmm.

Here we have: facilities by birth sex (broad: bathrooms, locker rooms, shelters, dorms, prisons), no remedy (no state discrimination law, religious refusal immunity), border document friction (visa refusal risk), federal custody abuse documented. No police targeting documented, no violence campaign, functioning courts partially mitigating (some measures enjoined).

I'd put it around 0.30-0.35. The border element (visa refusal, stranded travelers) adds exposure beyond the pure-facility anchors. But no documented enforcement of the state statute against visitors, and rule of law functions (courts blocking things, national employment protection, hate crime statute).

I'll say 0.32.

Let me think about band: 0.20-0.40 High Risk. Given tier-1 universal exposure with no working remedy plus custody exposure plus border friction, high risk seems right. 0.30-0.35.

Anchor 0.35-C had police extortion targeting; 0.35-B birth-sex placement in hospitals/detention with documented harm. Our case: facility ban (all public buildings incl. rest stops), custody placement by birth sex plus federal conversion policy for trans inmates — documented harm in custody (federal: denial of care, hair, hormones). That's documented harm in custody, though for residents/inmates mostly; immigration custody abuse documented (trans men forced labour, beatings, sexual abuse) — immigration detainees could include visitors overstaying/being detained. That's state-perpetrated severe harm.

Hmm, that pushes lower — immigration custody abuse of trans detainees is traveler-relevant (a visitor could be detained at border if visa refused... actually denial of entry usually means removal, but detained trans visitors documented? The dossier says trans travelers' passports confiscated/stranded). Federal immigration custody abuse of trans men is documented — that's a state-perpetrated severe exposure for any trans person entering immigration custody.

So: tier 1 facility exclusion + tier 2 state-tolerated/directed custody harm + border document exposure + no remedy. That suggests ~0.28-0.32.

I'll go with 0.30.
